{{Short description|Mechanical linkage transforming rotary motion into linear}}
{{more footnotes|date=August 2017}}
[[File:Peaucellier-Lipkin Inversor.gif|thumb|Animation for Peaucellier–Lipkin linkage:<br><br>Dimensions:<br>Cyan Links = a<br>Green Links = b<br>Yellow Links = c]]
The '''Peaucellier&ndash;Lipkin linkage''' (or '''Peaucellier&ndash;Lipkin cell''', or '''Peaucellier&ndash;Lipkin inversor'''), invented in 1864, was the first true planar [[straight-line mechanism]]{{snd}}the first planar [[linkage (mechanical)|linkage]] capable of transforming [[rotary motion]] into perfect [[straight-line motion]], and vice versa. It is named after [[Charles-Nicolas Peaucellier]] (1832&ndash;1913), a French army officer, and [[Yom Tov Lipman Lipkin]] (1846&ndash;1876), a [[Lithuanian Jew]] and son of the famed Rabbi [[Israel Salanter]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://kmoddl.library.cornell.edu/tutorials/11/ |title=Mathematical tutorial of the Peaucellier–Lipkin linkage |publisher=Kmoddl.library.cornell.edu |accessdate=2011-12-06}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|last=Taimina |first=Daina |url=https://kmoddl.library.cornell.edu/tutorials/04/ |title=How to draw a straight line by Daina Taimina |publisher=Kmoddl.library.cornell.edu |accessdate=2011-12-06}}</ref>

Until this invention, no planar method existed of converting exact straight-line motion to circular motion without reference guideways. In 1864, all power came from [[steam engine]]s, a steam engine having a [[piston]] moving in a straight line within a cylinder. This piston needed to keep a good seal with the cylinder in order to retain the driving medium and not lose energy efficiency due to leaks. The piston does this by remaining perpendicular to the axis of the cylinder, retaining its straight-line motion. Converting the straight-line motion of the piston into circular motion was of critical importance. Most, if not all, applications of these steam engines were rotary.

The mathematics of the Peaucellier&ndash;Lipkin linkage is directly related to the [[inversive geometry|inversion]] of a circle.

==Earlier Sarrus linkage==
There is an earlier straight-line mechanism, whose history is not well known, called the [[Sarrus linkage]]. This linkage predates the Peaucellier&ndash;Lipkin linkage by 11 years and consists of a series of hinged rectangular plates, two of which remain parallel but can be moved normally to each other. Sarrus' linkage is of a three-dimensional class sometimes known as a [[space crank]], unlike the Peaucellier&ndash;Lipkin linkage, which is a planar mechanism.

==Geometry==
[[File:PeaucellierApparatus.PNG|thumb|right|Geometric diagram of a Peaucellier linkage]]
In the geometric diagram of the apparatus, six bars of fixed length can be seen: {{mvar|{{overline|OA}}}}, {{mvar|{{overline|OC}}}}, {{mvar|{{overline|AB}}}}, {{mvar|{{overline|BC}}}}, {{mvar|{{overline|CD}}}}, {{mvar|{{overline|DA}}}}. The length of {{mvar|{{overline|OA}}}} is equal to the length of {{mvar|{{overline|OC}}}}, and the lengths of {{mvar|{{overline|AB}}}}, {{mvar|{{overline|BC}}}}, {{mvar|{{overline|CD}}}}, and {{mvar|{{overline|DA}}}} are all equal, forming a [[rhombus]].  Also, point {{mvar|O}} is fixed.  Then, if point {{mvar|B}} is constrained to move along a circle (for example, by attaching it to a bar with a length halfway between {{mvar|O}} and {{mvar|B}}; path shown in red) which passes through {{mvar|O}}, then point {{mvar|D}} will necessarily have to move along a straight line (shown in blue).  In contrast, if point {{mvar|B}} were constrained to move along a line (not passing through {{mvar|O}}), then point {{mvar|D}} would necessarily have to move along a circle (passing through {{mvar|O}}).

Many different overall proportions of this linkage are possible.  Since points {{mvar|O}}, {{mvar|B}}, {{mvar|D}} must be collinear at all points in the linkage's motion, and countless arm length combinations are viable, then mirror symmetry across {{mvar|{{overline|OBD}}}} isn't necessary.  With {{mvar|{{overline|OBD}}}} staying collinear, the only requirement to achieve the intended straight-line motion of {{mvar|D}} are that {{math|1={{overline|AB}} = {{overline|AD}}}}, that {{math|1={{overline|BC}} = {{overline|DC}}}}, and for {{mvar|B}} to be constrained to a circular path which crosses {{mvar|O}}.  Otherwise, there is no fixed relationship between the lengths of the sides of the {{mvar|ABCD}} figure, the radius of the constraining circular path of {{mvar|B}}, and the lengths of {{mvar|{{overline|OA}}}} or {{mvar|{{overline|OC}}}}.

==Mathematical proof of concept==

===Collinearity===
First, it must be proven that points {{mvar|O}}, {{mvar|B}}, {{mvar|D}} are [[Collinearity|collinear]].  This may be easily seen by observing that the linkage is mirror-symmetric about line {{mvar|OD}}, so point {{mvar|B}} must fall on that line.

More formally, triangles {{math|△''BAD''}} and {{math|△''BCD''}} are congruent because side {{mvar|{{overline|BD}}}} is congruent to itself, side {{mvar|{{overline|BA}}}}  is congruent to side {{mvar|{{overline|BC}}}} , and side {{mvar|{{overline|AD}}}}  is congruent to side {{mvar|{{overline|CD}}}} .  Therefore, angles {{math|∠''ABD''}} and {{math|∠''CBD''}} are equal.

Next, triangles {{math|△''OBA''}} and {{math|△''OBC''}} are congruent, since sides {{mvar|{{overline|OA}}}} and {{mvar|{{overline|OC}}}}  are congruent, side {{mvar|{{overline|OB}}}} is congruent to itself, and sides {{mvar|{{overline|BA}}}}  and {{mvar|{{overline|BC}}}}  are congruent.  Therefore, angles {{math|∠''OBA''}} and {{math|∠''OBC''}} are equal.

Finally, because they form a complete circle, we have
:<math> \angle OBA + \angle ABD + \angle DBC + \angle CBO = 360^\circ</math>

but, due to the congruences, {{math|1=∠''OBA'' = ∠''OBC''}} and {{math|1=∠''DBA'' = ∠''DBC''}}, thus
:<math>\begin{align}
& 2 \times \angle OBA + 2 \times \angle DBA = 360^\circ \\
& \angle OBA + \angle DBA = 180^\circ
\end{align}</math>

therefore points {{mvar|O}}, {{mvar|B}}, and {{mvar|D}} are collinear.

===Inverse points===
Let point {{mvar|P}} be the intersection of lines {{mvar|AC}} and {{mvar|BD}}.  Then, since {{mvar|ABCD}} is a [[rhombus]], {{mvar|P}} is the [[midpoint]] of both line segments {{mvar|{{overline|BD}}}} and {{mvar|{{overline|AC}}}}.  Therefore, length {{mvar|{{overline|BP}}}} = length {{mvar|{{overline|PD}}}}.

Triangle {{math|△''BPA''}} is congruent to triangle {{math|△''DPA''}}, because side {{mvar|{{overline|BP}}}} is congruent to side {{mvar|{{overline|DP}}}}, side {{mvar|{{overline|AP}}}} is congruent to itself, and side {{mvar|{{overline|AB}}}} is congruent to side {{mvar|{{overline|AD}}}} .  Therefore, angle {{math|∠''BPA''}} = angle {{math|∠''DPA''}}.  But since {{math|1=∠''BPA'' + ∠''DPA'' = 180°}}, then {{math|1=2 × ∠''BPA'' = 180°}}, {{math|1=∠''BPA'' = 90°}}, and {{math|1=∠''DPA'' = 90°}}.

Let:
:<math>\begin{align}
& x = \ell_{BP} = \ell_{PD} \\
& y = \ell_{OB} \\
& h = \ell_{AP}
\end{align}</math>

Then:
:<math>\ell_{OB}\cdot \ell_{OD}=y(y+2x)=y^2+2xy </math>
:<math>{\ell_{OA}}^2 = (y + x)^2 + h^2</math> <small>(due to the [[Pythagorean theorem]])</small>
:<math>{\ell_{OA}}^2 = y^2 + 2xy + x^2 + h^2</math><small>(same expression expanded)</small>
:<math>{\ell_{AD}}^2 = x^2 + h^2</math> <small>(Pythagorean theorem)</small>
:<math>{\ell_{OA}}^2 - {\ell_{AD}}^2 = y^2 + 2xy = \ell_{OB} \cdot \ell_{OD}</math>

Since {{mvar|{{overline|OA}}}} and {{mvar|{{overline|AD}}}}  are both fixed lengths, then the product of {{mvar|{{overline|OB}}}}  and {{mvar|{{overline|OD}}}} is a constant:
:<math>\ell_{OB}\cdot \ell_{OD} = k^2 </math>

and since points {{mvar|O}}, {{mvar|B}}, {{mvar|D}} are collinear, then {{mvar|D}} is the inverse of {{mvar|B}} with respect to the circle {{math|(O,''k'')}} with center {{mvar|O}} and radius {{mvar|k}}.

===Inversive geometry===
Thus, by the properties of [[inversive geometry]], since the figure traced by point {{mvar|D}} is the inverse of the figure traced by point {{mvar|B}}, if {{mvar|B}} traces a circle passing through the center of inversion {{mvar|O}}, then {{mvar|D}} is constrained to trace a straight line.  But if {{mvar|B}} traces a straight line not passing through {{mvar|O}}, then {{mvar|D}} must trace an arc of a circle passing through {{mvar|O}}. ''[[Q.E.D.]]''

===A typical driver===
[[File:The Peaucellier-Lipkin linkage with a rocker-slider four-bar as its driver.gif|thumb|right|Slider-rocker four-bar acts as the driver of the Peaucellier–Lipkin linkage]]
Peaucellier–Lipkin linkages (PLLs) may have several inversions. A typical example is shown in the opposite figure, in which a rocker-slider four-bar serves as the input driver. To be precise, the slider acts as the input, which in turn drives the right grounded link of the PLL, thus driving the entire PLL.

===Historical notes===
[[James Joseph Sylvester|Sylvester]] (''Collected Works'', Vol. 3, Paper 2) writes that when he showed a model to [[Lord Kelvin|Kelvin]], he “nursed it as if it had been his own child, and when a motion was made to relieve him of it, replied ‘No! I have not had nearly enough of it—it is the most beautiful thing I have ever seen in my life.’”

==Cultural references==
A monumental-scale sculpture implementing the linkage in illuminated struts is on permanent exhibition in [[Eindhoven, Netherlands]]. The artwork measures {{convert|22|x|15|x|16|m}}, weighs {{convert|6600|kg}}, and can be operated from a [[control panel (engineering)|control panel]] accessible to the general public.<ref name="Schoofs">{{cite web|title=Just because you are a character, doesn't mean you have character|url=https://ivoschoofs.com/project/just-because-you-are-a-character-doesnt-mean-you-have-character/|website=Ivo Schoofs|accessdate=2017-08-14|archive-date=2020-12-02|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201202060715/https://ivoschoofs.com/project/just-because-you-are-a-character-doesnt-mean-you-have-character/|url-status=dead}}</ref>
